body.rationale: The governing IPS is a draft, so I weight compliance as provisional but still prefer portfolios the CIO can build from. First choice is resampled_efficient_frontier. It has no hard IPS breaches, and its 13.3 effective N spreads the CMA risk. Its backtest Sharpe is 0.63 and its drawdown is -24.3%. Its reviewers praised internal consistency and candour about the gamma tuning. Its weaknesses are thin drawdown headroom and an unbiased-CMA assumption, which the CIO can manage. Second is black_litterman. It is clean on the IPS, has 6.1 effective N, a 0.70 backtest Sharpe, and a verified execution. The reviews flagged only a boundary-tuned volatility and a mechanism claim. Third is pc_researcher. It has the best ex-ante Sharpe among the diversified options (0.51), a backtest Sharpe of 0.70, a -10.9% drawdown, and only two soft breaches, volatility and tracking error. Reviewers noted a mismatch between its narrative and its delivered output, so it ranks below the two compliant return-optimised portfolios. Fourth is cvar_minimization. It is compliant, uses actual tail scenarios, and has the best backtest Sharpe (0.74). Its weaknesses are fitting to a few crises and 2.9 effective N. Fifth is max_sharpe. It is compliant with the highest compliant ex-ante Sharpe (0.46). It ranks last of my five because 46% in us_value rests on one judged CMA gap, and its drawdown is -24.7%. My first choice beats my fifth because it is more diffuse (13.3 vs 3.8 effective N), so it does not depend on one return gap. That favours covariance-robust construction over forecast-concentrated bets. As an adversarial diversifier I know a corner portfolio is only useful as an ensemble component. For that reason I flag hierarchical_risk_parity. It is 92% cash with 1.4 effective N and three hard breaches. The intra-category reviewer found a technical error (capital split vs risk budget). The inter-category reviewer attacked the premise that low realised volatility means low risk. The CIO should not lean on it. I did not flag my peers' other near-cash portfolios, because they carry similar structural weaknesses but at least have some diversification.
